draft.title: Imagery
card: Imagery is language that appeals to the senses. It helps a reader see, hear, smell, taste or feel a scene.
A writer picks specific details instead of general words. "Burnt toast and wet dog" is more vivid than "a bad smell".
Imagery can use more than one sense at once. Sight, sound, smell, taste and touch together make a scene feel real.
The effect is to place the reader inside the experience, so they feel it rather than only being told about it. The details chosen can also shape how the reader feels about the scene.
draft.remember: Imagery uses sense details to make a reader experience a scene, not just read about it.

a.q: Which sentence is the best example of imagery?
opts: Cold rain stung her cheeks and soaked her thin socks
The weather was very unpleasant that afternoon
She did not like being outside in the rain
It rained for most of the day on Tuesday
a.why: The first sentence uses touch details, stinging cheeks and soaked socks, so the reader can feel the scene. The others only state facts or opinions, with no sense details.
a.clue: Which sentence lets you feel the scene, not just hear a fact?

b.q: Read: "Onions sizzled and popped, and a sweet smell filled the hall." What is the main effect of this imagery?
opts: It places the reader in the scene through sound and smell
It tells the reader the cook is very skilled
It gives the reader facts about how onions are cooked
It shows the writer is angry about the cooking
b.why: Sizzled and popped appeal to hearing, and the sweet smell appeals to smell. Together they put the reader in the room. The sentence gives no information about the cook's skill, which is the most tempting wrong idea.
b.clue: Which senses does the sentence use?
